strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying persuasive communication as a critical gap in existing SDG agents
Conceptually interesting Stackelberg competition formulation providing intuitive grounding for turn-based dialogue
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse SDGs with 4-5 baselines per game
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of complete reward function and training-based vs prompt-based refinement
Demonstrated generalization across different backend LLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B) without retraining
Pragmatic two-stage architecture leveraging both API-based and open-source LLMs
Clear presentation with informative figures and qualitative case studies
weaknesses: Loose application of Stackelberg theory: claims local leader-follower optimization leads to global game success but provides only intuition, not rigorous proof (Eq. 13)
Critical train-test information mismatch: rewards computed with full information (rt+1) during training but unavailable at inference, creating significant distribution shift
Validity of Measurer as reward signal questionable: frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct assumed to accurately model followers using different LLMs, but variable generalization (Figure 4) suggests otherwise
Unfair baseline comparisons: Refiner applied on top of existing baselines adds optimization layer baseline authors didn't access; no equivalent computational budget comparison
Self-play dataset potential bias: training data from only 3 LLMs may optimize for their specific instruction-following patterns rather than general persuasion principles
Limited analysis of learned behaviors: no linguistic pattern analysis, no failure cases, unsupported claims about learning 'model-agnostic principles'
Incomplete reproducibility: prompt sensitivity not analyzed, hyperparameter selection (LoRA rank 16, n=8, β=0.04) not justified, no code/data release, dependency on proprietary models
Reward function concerns: no analysis of edge cases (very high/low probabilities), potential issues with different target response lengths, token probability normalization
Evaluation gaps: no confidence intervals or significance tests for reported performance differences; unclear agent sampling procedure in evaluation games

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine gap in SDG literature by focusing on persuasive communication rather than just strategy selection
Clear and intuitive methodology: Three-step framework (Intent Identification, Impact Measurement, Strategy Optimization) is well-designed and easy to follow
Pragmatic technical approach: Uses GRPO to avoid preference data/critic models; two-stage architecture leveraging API and open-source LLMs is effective

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Four benchmarks, multiple strong baselines, ablations on reward variants and hyperparameters, cross-LLM generalization studies, human evaluation with proper protocols, qualitative case studies, and persuasion effectiveness analysis
Consistent improvements across domains: Gains demonstrated across Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW, and Sotopia, suggesting reasonable generalizability
Good reproducibility support: Clear implementation details, hyperparameters, training procedures, and prompts in appendices; code/data release promised
weaknesses: Weak theoretical foundation: Claim that local Stackelberg optimization creates beneficial cascade lacks rigorous justification; counterexamples exist (utterances convincing next player but alienating later players); relationship to global game outcomes is informal first-order approximation

Train-test mismatch on hidden information: Method uses next player's hidden role r_{t+1} during reward computation at training time but not at inference; justification is circular; no analysis of performance degradation from this mismatch

Modest and inconsistent improvements: Gains range from 2.6-6.1% across games; some configurations show degradation (Avalon Good: 70.5%→73.1% is improvement but context shows variance); no statistical significance testing despite 500 matches per game
Computational cost and scalability: Requires 50 GPU-hours per game; necessitates training separate model per scenario; limits practical applicability to new domains

Reward signal design concerns: K=3 is empirically validated but somewhat arbitrary; using Qwen2.5-72B to approximate Gemini-2.5-Flash responses is unvalidated approximation; intent identification via prompting is non-deterministic and sensitivity is unexplored

Utterance length confound: Paper acknowledges training increases utterance length; no analysis of whether improvements stem from persuasion or simply from verbosity providing more information; no length penalty during training

Limited and potentially ambiguous human evaluation: Only 16 participants with 5 games each; fewer votes received could indicate avoidance due to suspicion rather than successful persuasion; no qualitative assessment of how persuasive vs. manipulative agents appeared
Weak ablations: No ablation on using hidden role information during training; no ablation on Measurer quality; no cross-game transfer experiments; no comparison of GRPO to PPO/DPO

Foundational assumptions not validated: No evidence that local optimization of immediate next-player response optimizes global game outcomes; trade-offs between convincing next player and maintaining credibility with others unexplored
